A #Python[1] string-literals gotcha I just ran into:
items.content:
A # string-literals gotcha I just ran into:

In a triple-quoted Python string, you can use the quote character if it appears once at a time:"""a string with "quoted text" in it"""

But if you put a quote character at the _end_ of the string, that fails:"""a string ending with "quoted text""""

because the _first_ three quotes of the final """" terminate the literal, and the fourth one is unmatched, and a syntax error.

Unless it's _not_ unmatched, because you had absentmindedly done this:"""<a href="""" + html.escape(url) + """">link text</a>"""

so that there's an even number of extra " characters and they match again.

The meaning of this code from Python's point of view is three consecutive string literals, implicitly concatenated:"""<a href=""" # triply-quoted

" + html.escape(url) + " # singly-quoted

""">link text</a>""" # triply-quoted

and the call to html.escape() in the middle, which was _supposed_ to be an actual function call, has silently become plain text, and you get no syntax error and a nonsense hyperlink.

items.title: Here's an example tiling, shown in both Spectre and metatiles view. The tiles are coloured to match their metatiles, so you can see which groups of four Spectres correspond to the 3-arms, and also see that the diabolos contributed no Spectres at all to the final tiling.
items.content:
Here's an example tiling, shown in both Spectre and metatiles view. The tiles are coloured to match their metatiles, so you can see which groups of four Spectres correspond to the 3-arms, and also see that the diabolos contributed no Spectres at all to the final tiling.

This is one of the two 6-way singular Spectre patterns: the lighter-coloured tiles, occupying most of the plane, have 6-way rotational symmetry about the centre point, with only the wiggly paths of darker tiles being asymmetric.

In the Spectre version, the asymmetric paths come in two forms, with large and small wiggles (of lowest order – as you zoom out those wiggles turn out to be accompanied by larger slower wiggles, and so on). In the metatiles version, the paths with larger wiggles to narrow paths of metatiles which vary only in orientation, while the paths with smaller wiggles correspond to thicker paths of metatiles which vary shape as well. However, under deflation, each of these types of path maps to the other one – the apparently larger amount of change in the thicker paths turns out to be mostly an illusion!

items.title: The substitution system of three tiles shown in the previous toot is all very well, but how does it relate to Spectres?
items.content:
The substitution system of three tiles shown in the previous toot is all very well, but how does it relate to Spectres?

To convert these tiles to Spectres, we begin by distorting each one, by varying the angle and length of one of the edge types relative to the other one. Two of the resulting outlines are self-intersecting, and the third (the diabolo) is actually inside-out.

(That makes the idea of tiling with them a bit weird, but the outlines do still _fit together_, even if it's confusing to try to work out how many tiles cover any given point in the plane.)

But with the right distortion, we can draw a consistent path of Spectre edges on each of the two edge types. The resulting outlines retrace their steps a lot, and it turns out that with those zero-thickness spurs ignored, the 2-arms outline traces exactly round a single Spectre tile, and the 3-arms round a patch that tiles with four Spectres (the middle one being one of the rare ones at an odd multiple of 30°).

Stranger than that is what happens to the diabolo: its _whole_ outline consists of zero-thickness spurs that double back on themselves, and it encloses no area at all. In this system of Spectre metatiles, one of the metatiles vanishes completely on the final conversion to Spectres!

items.title: Just up on arXiv, a preprint presenting a 'D23' system of three metatiles that generate the Spectre tiling. Follows on from some work with Marianne Impéror-Clerc and Jean-François Sadoc.
items.content:
Just up on arXiv, a preprint presenting a 'D23' system of three metatiles that generate the Spectre tiling. Follows on from some work with Marianne Impéror-Clerc and Jean-François Sadoc.

The three metatiles are shown here, with the substitution rule that turns each edge type into a set of smaller edges, and how the resulting more crinkly outlines are filled with smaller copies of the same metatiles (reflected, as usual).

The shapes of the metatiles look symmetric, but the edge orientations are not quite. As a result, the deflated outlines are also asymmetric in the same places, though you have to look twice to spot it.

items.title: The fifth escape sequence in the switch, ESC # 8, is one of the most fun ones in the whole terminal. It instantly replaces the entire screen contents with copies of the capital letter E.
items.content:
The fifth escape sequence in the switch, ESC # 8, is one of the most fun ones in the whole terminal. It instantly replaces the entire screen contents with copies of the capital letter E.

In DEC's documentation it goes by the name DECALN, and is described as an alignment test. I guess the point is that it's a quick way to put text in every part of the screen, if you're about to check that your old-fashioned CRT monitor is showing the whole of the terminal contents, and not e.g. missing half a row or column because it's off one edge of the display.

I was fascinated by that sequence as a child, partly because it's amusing, and also because of the way that it _instantly_ updated the screen, which I didn't know how to do any other way (the machines I was using were slow and I was writing in high-level languages). It stuck in my head all my life for that reason.

And I eventually found a real use for it! Once I wanted to train myself out of the bad habit of using backticks in my shell commands (the synonym $(...) is better, because it nests sensibly and doesn't impose extra escaping needs on its interior). So I bound the ` key in bash to a command that echoed ESC#8, which was just the right level of reminder to not do that again – it didn't make a loud noise annoying my colleagues, or destroy any work, but it definitely reminded me to change that habit. After about a month, I'd got into the new habit and removed the binding.

items.title: This code was in PuTTY for less than a year. But in that time it managed to expose a bug in a C compiler.
items.content:
This code was in PuTTY for less than a year. But in that time it managed to expose a bug in a C compiler.

It was a small, independently written compiler (none of the huge code bases everyone's heard of now). We had an email from its maintainer to let us know – and to ask us what the code was _meant_ to do, because fair enough, it isn't obvious to everybody at first glance!

The bug was that the compiler optimised away if (0) { ... } statements, on the theory that they were unreachable. But the code in these if (0) statements _is_ reachable, via the case labels related to the containing switch. So the compiler had thrown away code that was actually needed, and then got confused when it couldn't generate the jump for those switch cases.

(The more usual strategy is to start by turning the whole function into a control-flow graph, i.e. blocks of straight-line code in a directed graph connected by edges that are effectively gotos. Then you can optimise conditional branches based on a constant into unconditional branches, deleting the never-traversed graph edge out of their block. Then you detect unreachable code by a search through the graph from the function entry point. That strategy avoids this problem.)

items.title: Reminded of this in conversation recently: possibly the nastiest piece of abuse of the C switch statement rules I know of that _wasn't_ done by either me or Tom Duff. This was contributed to #PuTTY[1]'s terminal code in 2000 as part of a much larger patch (and removed again in a 2001 rewrite).
items.content:
Reminded of this in conversation recently: possibly the nastiest piece of abuse of the C switch statement rules I know of that _wasn't_ done by either me or Tom Duff. This was contributed to #'s terminal code in 2000 as part of a much larger patch (and removed again in a 2001 rewrite).

The switch is processing the final character of one of the terminal escape sequences ESC#3, ESC#4, ESC#5, ESC#6 and ESC#8. Four of them do something very similar: they set an attribute on the current terminal line (indicating whether the text is double-width or double-height). The fifth is the odd one out. So you want a switch statement in which four of the five cases share _most_ of their code: each sets the line attribute to a different value, but the code for actually writing it into the terminal is the same.

You could write four case statements sharing a handler, and have a secondary switch inside the handler to choose the attribute. Or you could have four separate handlers that choose an attribute value, then hold your nose and write a 'goto' from each one to the shared code that writes it into the terminal data. Or you could put the shared code in a subroutine a long way away from here, and have four independent case handlers all call it with a different parameter.

Or you could do this, which complies with the letter of 'don't use goto', but makes you wish it hadn't! Control enters at one of the four case statements, and after setting the attribute variable, it then skips over each of the following case labels because of the if (0) { ... }. Then all of them fall through to the shared handler.

Sometimes the most important use of a software feature isn't the one you originally expected it to be.

I have a personal downstream hack on 'gitk' which adds an extra entry to the context menu when you right-click on part of the patch: "Open this line in emacs." (It talks to my running Emacs via the emacs-server Unix socket and tells it what filename + line number to open. Saves me retyping the pathname and trying to find the corresponding line by hand.)

I expected that the use of this would be looking at more context around a patch hunk I'm trying to understand, or going to the location where a previous patch had introduced a bug so as to fix it.

But in fact, 90% of the time, I just use it as the quickest way to get back to whatever I left half-done yesterday when I finished work: cd into the checkout, run gitk, right-click on the uncommitted changes or the most recent commit.

items.title: Reading some C++ code, I quickly jotted down an expression or two on paper so that I'd remember it when I went to the other end of the file to compare it with something else. (Yes, I still keep pencil and paper by my computer, I'm old-fashioned that way.)
items.content:
Reading some C++ code, I quickly jotted down an expression or two on paper so that I'd remember it when I went to the other end of the file to compare it with something else. (Yes, I still keep pencil and paper by my computer, I'm old-fashioned that way.)

The expression involved the && operator, which is a pain to handwrite. One & is complicated enough; two are just ridiculous. I idly started trying to doodle a joined-up glyph that combined two of them.

About 20 attempts later, tada! I present the "ampersampersand".

You can handwrite it in a single stroke, but it's tricky at first, because the two upper loops have to be drawn in opposite directions. But even so, it's quicker to write than two separate ampersands.

Now I'm half tempted to draw a version for my personal font and add it as a ligature to see how that goes.

items.title: A thing that really annoys me about English idiom is that when people name the four cardinal directions, they tend to say "east and west" rather than "west and east" – but they tend to say "left and right" rather than "right and left". And (in the usual north-at-the-top map orientation) those are opposite ways round.
items.content:
A thing that really annoys me about English idiom is that when people name the four cardinal directions, they tend to say "east and west" rather than "west and east" – but they tend to say "left and right" rather than "right and left". And (in the usual north-at-the-top map orientation) those are opposite ways round.

I've always struggled to tell east from west. Whenever I have to translate a spoken direction into something on a map, or vice versa, I always have to stop and think twice to make sure I haven't got them backwards. I have some mnemonics, like "west rhymes with left", or mentally zooming the map out until I can see America and Russia (and I know which of _those_ is "the West"), but they're not instantaneous, and I always have to slow down to check them.

I'm convinced that this reversal in the default speech order is the reason. If my whole life I'd heard "west/east" and "left/right", I would have had no trouble matching up the one that comes first in both forms.

It especially annoys me when _I_ name the directions in those orders. After I've decided it's wrong and bad, you'd think I ought at least to be able to shake the habit myself! But I said 'east, west' again this morning without thinking and kicked myself.

items.title: I often find typos cognitively fascinating.
items.content:
I often find typos cognitively fascinating.

Some typos are just last-moment motor errors: "aimed for this key and hit the one next to it". Those are easy to understand. But others reveal much more interesting things about the mental process of driving your fingers on the keyboard, or even composing words.

I once aimed to type 'programs', and unexpectedly 'rpgroasm' came out. All the left-hand letters appear in the correct order, and so do all the right-hand letters, but they're interleaved in a spectacularly wrong way. That suggested that one part of my brain had sent an independent set of instructions to a subthing controlling each hand, and everything worked fine except the synchronisation between the two subthings.

There's another class of typo which I think of as 'brain got ahead of fingers': you're typing one word, but already thinking about a word that will come after it, and there's a crossover and you end up mixing up the two. Like 'bit bisect' in place of 'git bisect' – you're already planning the b, and it comes out of your fingers prematurely.

(Appropriately, as I typed _that_ sentence, 'in place' came out as 'pl inace', wow.)

Even the 'boring' motor errors have something cognitively interesting about them, just on the reading rather than writing side. We see 'adjacent letter on the keyboard' typos a lot, so our brains get good at correcting them. Sometimes _over_-correcting, so that you imagine a typo where none existed. When a sentence is a bit unexpected in context, I've been known to consider the possibility of a typo before figuring out how the sentence as originally spelled makes sense.

The best ones of those are when I hadn't even _realised_ the two words were a typo apart. I misread 'auction' as 'suction' once and it was a total surprise!

I wonder if there's any serious scholarly study of this kind of thing.
